history.title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
history.text: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts. Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent. F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround. The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company. None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself. Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition. Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server: - CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only. - CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. - CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. - CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. - CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. - CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected. F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX. For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed. The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work. A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team. BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285. The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe. Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings. Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1: - CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups. - CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed. - CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws. - CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks. - CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact. - CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.
history.summary: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until restart, and may allow remote code execution. Each flaw requires a specific virtual server setup: an iRule using a particular command or an APM policy with certain agents, affecting modules like DNS, PEM, APM, and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes/CNF. F5 has released engineering hotfixes as the only fix, with no workaround available, and the hotfixes come with no warranty or promise of full QA validation.

history.title: Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials
history.text: Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz. The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access. Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python. "Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report. Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported. "Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework." The names of the .pth files are below - - agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1 - af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2 The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data - - Environment variables based on substring-based matching - Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files - Azure DevOps OIDC tokens - Azure managed-identity tokens - Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response "Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those." "In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata." It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token. All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb"). Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables. Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps - - Isolate affected hosts and runners - Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment - Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026 - Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb - Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system - Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs - Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure "The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside." Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.
history.summary: Threat actors compromised Microsoft's agent-framework PyPI package, releasing malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 that install Python startup hooks to silently steal credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens. The malicious .pth files exfiltrate collected data zlib-compressed and Base64-encoded to a webhook.site endpoint, affecting environments even without explicit package import. As of November 17, 2026, both malicious versions were quarantined on PyPI, and users are advised to pin to version 1.26.0, rotate exposed credentials, and audit Azure and GitHub Actions identities.

history.title: Data breach impacts 40 Irish credit unions in reported IT provider hack
history.text: A reported cyberattack on Wellington IT has exposed sensitive information belonging to members of 50 credit unions, the majority of which are located in Ireland. Wellington IT is a Belfast-based supplier whose services are used by about 50 credit unions, including 43 in Ireland. While the company has not publicly disclosed a security incident, Minister of State Robert Troy confirmed to RTÉ that Wellington IT is the third-party service provider linked to the cybersecurity incident involving credit unions, resulting in the exposure of data from about 40 credit unions in Ireland. The company reportedly notified affected organizations of a data breach that posed a risk of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing to their members. According to the Irish Examiner, which saw the notices, Wellington IT informed customers that an automated script made five million requests to exploit an authorization flaw in the company's infrastructure. The attack unfolded between October 2 and 4, 2026, and the attacker accessed private records using valid credentials. However, the firm said it lacked activity logs that would specify which member data was compromised and therefore cannot verify the impact on individual payees. Minister R. Troy characterized the massive delay in Wellington IT notifying the credit unions as "not acceptable." At this time, the total number of impacted individuals is unknown. Sensitive information exposed At least six credit unions have independently disclosed impact linked to the incident, including Capital Credit Union, Phoenix Credit Union, St. Canice's Credit Union, First South Credit Union, Malahide Credit Union, and Limerick & District Credit Union. The announcements confirmed unauthorized access to payee information, with some noting that members' login credentials and funds haven't been affected, while others are working to determine exactly what was exposed. The notices list the following payee records saved in online banking platforms as potentially exposed: - Payee name or name associated with the payee's bank account - Nickname the member used to save the payee, if provided - International Bank Account Number (IBAN) - Bank Identifier Code (BIC) - Bank account number - Bank sort code - Payee address information - Payment reference information entered for the saved payee The records could also reveal which credit union member saved a particular payee. Account passwords, PINs, payment card details, and online banking credentials were unaffected, but union members are advised to remain vigilant for phishing and impersonation attempts. BleepingComputer has contacted Wellington IT to learn more about the incident, and we will update this post with their response once we receive it. The company confirmed the breach posed risks of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing, but lacked activity logs to specify which member records were compromised, and at least six credit unions independently verified unauthorized access to payee information such as names, IBANs, and bank details. Minister Robert Troy called the delayed notification "not acceptable."

history.title: From Deepfakes to Helpdesk Impersonation: Why Stronger Verification Matters
history.text: In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup was tricked into transferring $25 million after attending a fake video conference featuring deepfake versions of their colleagues. A year later, Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack after attackers used social engineering to gain access through a third-party helpdesk. More recently, attackers have impersonated IT support staff to convince employees to hand over remote access to their devices. While the tactics differ, these incidents raise an important question for IT and security teams: how can organizations be confident that someone requesting access or authorizing a sensitive action is who they claim to be? We examine these attacks and explore how stronger identity verification and more secure workflows can help organizations defend against similar threats. The Arup Deepfake Fraud A finance employee at engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office received an email in January 2024 that appeared to come from the company's UK-based CFO, requesting a series of transactions. Initially suspicious, the employee was convinced the request was genuine after joining a video conference featuring what appeared to be the CFO and several colleagues. However, the meeting was a deepfake. According to Hong Kong police, the attackers had used publicly available video and audio to create a convincing pre-recorded conference. The employee subsequently made multiple transfers, losing approximately HK$200 million (US$25.6 million). The M&S Cyberattack In April 2025, British retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack that disrupted operations for weeks. Online orders were suspended, contactless payments and Click & Collect services were affected, and customer data was stolen. M&S initially estimated the incident would reduce its 2025/26 operating profit by around £300 million before mitigation. The attack was linked to the Scattered Spider cybercriminal group, known for using social engineering to gain access to corporate networks. M&S later confirmed that attackers had gained entry by deceiving employees at a third-party contractor, rather than exploiting a technical vulnerability in its systems. Fake IT Support Microsoft recently reported a cyberattack campaign in which threat actors impersonated IT support staff through Microsoft Teams, tricking employees into handing over remote access to their devices. The attackers contacted employees through external Teams messages or calls, posing as internal IT personnel. Using convincing pretexts such as urgent technical issues, they persuaded employees to grant remote control through screen sharing or legitimate support tools like Quick Assist. Once connected, the attackers used PowerShell to install malicious software, establish persistent access and gather information about the compromised network. Microsoft also observed attempts to move laterally towards critical infrastructure, including domain controllers and certificate authorities. The Common Thread: Trust Replacing Verification Impersonation Exploits Familiar Trust Signals Social engineering has long been a key technique in attackers’ arsenals. They don't need sophisticated malware or technical exploits to compromise an organization if they can convince someone that they're a trusted colleague. Deepfake technology makes this particularly concerning, as familiar faces and voices can be recreated. But even without AI, attackers can use convincing pretexts and trusted communication platforms to make fraudulent requests appear legitimate. Trusted Processes Can Become Attack Vectors Password resets and remote IT support are routine activities, but they can also give attackers opportunities to gain access if requests aren't properly verified. Third-party providers expand the potential attack surface; organizations may have strong controls over their own systems but less visibility into how external support teams verify identities and authorize sensitive actions. Employees Can't Be Expected to Spot Every Impersonation Attempt Security awareness training helps employees recognize suspicious requests, but even well-trained staff can be deceived by convincing impersonation attempts. Attackers will carry out reconnaissance beforehand to gather information that makes their social engineering attempts appear like routine requests. Organizations need reliable verification processes that support employees when they're asked to make security-sensitive decisions, rather than leaving them to judge whether someone can be trusted. How Can Organizations Mitigate These Risks? Build Verification Into Business Workflows As organizations introduce self-service portals, internal chatbots and automated IT processes, it's important that these systems follow the same verification standards as traditional support channels. By integrating verification directly into these processes, organizations can apply consistent security checks at critical points without relying entirely on manual intervention. Independently Verify Sensitive Requests For financial transactions, privileged access, and other sensitive requests, organizations should require independent confirmation through trusted channels. This might include contacting the requester using previously verified details or introducing additional authentication into approval workflows. Verify IT Support Requests Before Granting Access Where support processes are managed through internal applications or automated workflows, additional identity verification can help ensure that sensitive requests are made by authorized users. These measures should be supported by broader security controls like phishing-resistant MFA and least-privilege access, while monitoring for suspicious account activity. Make Strong Verification Part of Everyday Security As social engineering tactics become more convincing, organizations can't rely on employees recognizing every fraudulent request. history.title: Russian APT Poses as Employee of Hacked Firm to Breach Another US Organization
history.text: Russia-linked APT Star Blizzard hacked a US organization by impersonating an employee at another US organization it had previously compromised, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports. Also tracked as Callisto, Cold Relic, Cold River, UNC4057, and Gossamer Bear, and active for over a decade, Star Blizzard has been formally associated by the US with Russia’s intelligence service FSB. The APT is known for mounting sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to collect information relevant to the Russian government, and to use victims’ data in attacks on subsequent targets. Star Blizzard “has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo,” Google says. In a recent attack against a US organization, Star Blizzard impersonated an employee of another organization it had breached months earlier. Google, which tracks the group as Cold Relic, believes the hackers likely used contact and relationship information obtained during the earlier intrusion to select and deceive their new target. The first organization was hit in late 2025, using the compromised credentials of a super admin account. The APT leveraged a residential proxy network close to the victim and relied on multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue to register a device to the victim’s tenant. Next, the group downloaded the organization’s entire cloud storage drive, accessed the admin console to fingerprint defenses and remove evidence of the initial intrusion, exported full employee lists, and launched a domain-wide export. According to Google, the group used passkeys, rogue MFA devices, and MFA backup codes to maintain persistent access to the victim organization for several months. It also exfiltrated emails and targeted cloud drive documents containing information of interest. “When the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed Cold Relic leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts,” Google says. The APT impersonated an employee at the victim organization to establish communication with the second victim organization via a secure messaging application. Ultimately, it shared phishing links designed to steal credentials and Entra ID authentication tokens, and used the secrets to register a new MFA device to the second organization’s SSO solution to retain access to the compromised account. “By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive,” Google says. To maintain persistence, the APT registered rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes, conducted aggressive data collection and exfiltration, and searched for credentials, employee information, email archives, documents, and any other information it could use in subsequent spear-phishing attacks. The threat actor also changed its profile name in the secure messaging application used in this intrusion, likely to reuse it in another attack. “Cold Relic’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners,” Google notes. history.title: Last of Five Defendants Sentenced in US Scattered Spider Hacking Case
history.text: A British Scattered Spider hacker will spend six years in a US federal prison for his part in a conspiracy to hack companies and take at least $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from individuals across the US. Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and has been held by US authorities since April 2025. He pleaded guilty in April 2026 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Between September 2021 and April 2023, the Scattered Spider group texted hundreds of phishing lures to staff at telecommunications, technology, interactive entertainment, cloud communications, and cryptocurrency companies. Links in the texts pointed to phishing websites where recipients were tricked into entering credentials and personal information. Login details captured by the cybercriminals ended up in a Telegram channel managed by Buchanan and an accomplice. With the stolen credentials, the hackers broke into employee accounts and company systems and took confidential information. That information helped them pinpoint and access cryptocurrency accounts and wallets owned by individuals. To defeat two-factor authentication, they took over victims’ phone numbers through SIM swaps, moving the numbers to devices under their control. The theft total has grown from the $8 million cited at the time of Buchanan’s plea. The court will hold a restitution hearing on December 11. Buchanan is the final defendant in the five-person case to receive a sentence. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both of Texas, were each given 45 months in September and August, respectively. Noah Michael Urban is serving 10 years in federal prison, while Joel Martin Evans received a two-year term. Earlier this year, two other Scattered Spider members, Thalha Jubair and Owen Flowers, were sentenced to jail in the United Kingdom for a cyberattack targeting Transport for London (TfL). history.title: Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of Sites
history.text: Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site. That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday. The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale. The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site. No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php. The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days. Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13. What to Do Now The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are: - Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13 - Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22 - Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22 The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts. Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge. Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule. In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches. The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement. Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027. This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.
history.summary: A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-132165) in Drupal core allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit the built-in installer under specific conditions, potentially leading to site takeover or remote code execution. Fixed versions have been released: Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13, with exploitation rated as complex and an existing proof-of-concept exploit noted. Fix: Update to the fixed Drupal versions and block or remove the /core/install.php installer file using web server configuration, .htaccess rules, or Composer scripts.

history.title: Critical VMware vCenter Flaw (CVSS 9.8) Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
history.text: A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today. Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says. In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing. The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant. The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use. Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract. None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says. There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses. The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online. One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2. The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310. Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor. The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass. The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.
history.summary: Critical VMware vCenter flaw CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) lets network attackers bypass authentication in the VMware Directory Service. history.title: CISA Warns of 4 Exploited Flaws Linked to Ransomware, Cryptomining, and LLMjacking Attacks
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. - CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. - CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI. - CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors. "An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash." The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs. "To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0." In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026. "Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said. "The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives." In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting. Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176." CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied. As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key." The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region. Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware. In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.
history.summary: CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, citing active exploitation linked to ransomware, cryptomining, and LLMjacking attacks. CVE-2026-90436 in Apache Axis allows unauthenticated remote code execution and has been exploited to deploy cryptocurrency miners, though the flaw remains unpatched as Axis 1.x is end-of-life, with migration to Axis 2 or applying a July 2026 commit recommended. CVE-2026-90817 in REDCap and CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM were also added due to evidence of exploitation for arbitrary code execution and LLMjacking campaigns targeting financial, retail, and technology organizations. CVE-2024-10441 in Synology DSM was exploited in ransomware attacks deploying C3RB3R ransomware, with federal agencies advised to apply mitigations by November 21, 2026 for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws, and by December 2, 2026 for the LiteLLM flaw.

history.title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
history.text: One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day. The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected. Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them. Why Appliances Are the Softer Target On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled. Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere. HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit. Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option. That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide. Risk Was the Hardest Call The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle. The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own. We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets. Defending What Runs on HTTP I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them. Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026. Note: This article has been written and contributed by Dr. Johannes Ullrich, Dean of Research at SANS Technology Institute.

history.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
history.text: Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6. Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging. Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered. Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies. An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system. Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says. The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after. According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network. After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information. F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says. F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor. To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack in a Russian-language press release. Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes. SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds. history.title: Critical NGINX ‘NGINX2Root’ bugs let attackers hijack servers
history.text: Two critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers, with researchers demonstrating how the flaws can be chained with a Linux kernel bug to gain root access. The two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities were discovered independently by researchers at Xint, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, and Rapid7, while Xint also discovered three additional NGINX RCE flaws. Censys later reproduced the underlying memory corruption conditions in four of the five flaws through lab testing, but did not achieve remote code execution. The first of the two "nginx2root" flaws is CVE-2026-123007, a flow-control bug that can corrupt memory in an NGINX worker. It impacts all versions from 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5, released in 2015. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution on a server hosting ordinary static files over HTTP/2 with TLS, while Xint demoed root access by chaining it with a separate Linux kernel flaw. Xint says the separate vulnerability affects the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem and can be used to escape an NGINX Docker container and gain root privileges on the underlying host. The second flaw is CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free problem that affects NGINX when it accepts HTTP/2 connections and proxies requests to a backend. It impacts all versions from 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. When the worker runs low on connection slots, it can close an active connection and free memory that a request still uses. Wiz also demonstrated remote code execution via CVE-2026-123633, but the firm is not publicly releasing its proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits at this time. The other three flaws the researchers discovered and F5 fixed are CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123634, and CVE-2026-113425, all use-after-free vulnerabilities affecting HTTP/3 reverse proxying, DNS resolution with subrequests, and mail proxy authentication, respectively. The flaws were fixed in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline. NGINX Plus users should update to versions 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. F5’s latest security update also addresses five more vulnerabilities not highlighted in the Wiz or Xint reports. The most notable is CVE-2026-118899, a high-severity issue that allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a worker to enter an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3, resulting in denial of service. For system administrators, it is recommended to upgrade immediately to the latest NGINX release, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 until an upgrade is possible. However, this mitigation only covers the two "nginx2root" flaws. Evaluating the risk Regarding the real exploitability risk of "nginx2root," security researcher Florian Roth says it's worse than Node2Shell and Java2Shell, but doesn’t appear to be an imminent threat for most NGINX deployments. Commenting on X, Roth said the flaws are exploitable in non-default configurations, warning that claims of widespread exposure based solely on NGINX version numbers are misleading. Xint previously reported that 98.9% of NGINX hosts disclosing recognizable versions were running software within the affected range, but this does not account for whether HTTP/2 is enabled or security fixes have been backported. The two HTTP/2 flaws require an unpatched server with HTTP/2 enabled on a listener an attacker can reach, while CVE-2026-123633 also requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend. Roth scanned a sample of a few hundred NGINX HTTPS endpoints from Shodan and found that roughly 66% of them support HTTP/2, but confirming actual exposure requires checking the server’s configuration and whether a fix has been backported. According to Censys' live exposure tracker, approximately 8.8 million NGINX services were potentially exposed to CVE-2026-123007 as of November 19, based on affected version numbers and HTTP/2 support. The company reports that more than 511,000 previously exposed services have already been patched or mitigated, while another 104 million NGINX services do not disclose their versions, making it difficult to determine whether they are affected. history.summary: Critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable servers, with researchers demonstrating chainable attacks to gain root access. The two HTTP/2 flaws are CVE-2026-123007, a flow-control bug affecting versions from 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5, and CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free issue impacting versions 1.19.7 through 1.31.8 when proxying HTTP/2 requests to a backend. Fixes were released in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline, with NGINX Plus users updating to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.

history.title: ThreatsDay: GPT-6.2 Jailbreak Flaws, BubbleLoader PNG Malware, $500M Ransom Demands + 17 More Stories
history.text: The easiest way to fool someone is to give them something they already expect. A job offer. A message about a service outage. A familiar app. Nothing looks strange at first. And that's the problem. This week's stories show how ordinary things are being used to steal data, spread malware, and get people to hand over access. There's another shift worth watching. AI is making some attacks easier to run and harder to spot. Stolen data can now be searched like a shopping catalog. Phishing emails can be tested and rewritten until they get through. At the same time, researchers are finding that even powerful AI systems have safety gaps of their own. And while everyone is watching the new tools, the old problems haven't gone anywhere. Third-party breaches, years of hidden spying, ransomware, and security fixes still need attention. Some stories are clever. Others are painfully simple. Here's what caught our attention this week. The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. - Faster, more secure AI coding Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Neon, its latest frontier model capable of delivering reasoning faster and more cost-efficiently. According to the company's DeepMind division, it also produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). "Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost-efficient than large frontier models," Google said. "Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge." Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program. - Major leap in AI cyber capabilities OpenAI has introduced GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol with a "significant jump" in cyber capabilities. "They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations," OpenAI said. "Like GPT‑6 Astra, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework." The company also said it has made defensive capabilities a core focus by allowing the models to write secure code from the start. The development comes amid a disclosure from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) that it developed a universal jailbreak against two pre-release versions of OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra in half the queries required for GPT-6 Astra, adding it identified a "substantial regression in jailbreak robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra." OpenAI has since addressed the regression. - Urgent WordPress security update WordPress has released WordPress 7.1.5 with fixes for multiple security issues. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately," WordPress said. The patches have also been backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). - Independent AI safety assessments OpenAI will embed independent evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot to help support its safety work. The embedded assessors will focus on model alignment and monitoring, training run monitoring, post-training alignment evaluations, and assessing "whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior." "Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases," the company said. "Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated." OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face. The pilot, however, limits how much researchers can disclose, with OpenAI reserving the right to redact evidence or confidential information to substantiate the outcome of their evaluations. - $500 million ransomware extortion case Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, a Kazak national, has been extradited from Italy to the U.S. to face charges for his alleged role in a ransomware and extortion conspiracy that targeted U.S. schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities. "Khlynovskiy and other members of the '8-Digits Team' repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information," said FBI Director Kash Patel. "This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands." The 8-Digits Team is said to have been affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware, and targeted victims in at least six states, including both schools and hospitals. Khlynovskiy was arrested in Italy in July 2025 while vacationing with his family. He is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges. - AI model extraction tactics exposed An exclusive report from Reuters has revealed that Chinese entities are adopting sophisticated methods to conduct distillation attacks against American AI models and use the outputs to train domestic rivals, according to a review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices, and government documents. "Chinese researchers [are] using U.S. models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models," the report said. - AI-driven stolen data marketplace A criminal marketplace promoted on underground forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, according to Hudson Rock. The seller has claimed registration for the service is open and free. "The reviewed listings present each computer with a description of its apparent owner, workplace, applications, and potentially valuable data," Hudson Rock said. "Buyers can search those descriptions using natural language and combine the results with filters such as country, operating system, and price. The result is a catalog in which a compromised machine can be presented as a clinic’s reception desk, a defense contractor's household computer, or a government employee's family workstation. The service is marketing the context around the stolen data as part of the product." - North Korean ransomware campaign The North Korean hacking group known as Kimsuky group has been observed distributing the Funhouse ransomware via a malicious Hangul document that was disguised as a resume. "The Funhouse ransomware was identified as a variant of previously disclosed endpoint ransomware, and the tools used in this attack — such as Quasar RAT — as well as the overall attack chain shared numerous similarities with Kimsuky’s endpoint ransomware distribution cases observed since the first half of 2026," AhnLab said. - Gemini chat retention extended Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change is expected to roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks. It marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period. "Even if Gemini History is turned off, future chats will still be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers," Google said in a revised policy update on November 17, 2026. The change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become increasingly capable. Anthropic and OpenAI, by comparison, have said they may keep temporary or incognito chats in ChatGPT and Claude for 30 days by default or up to 30 days. - €11 million data privacy penalty Ireland's data protection regulator said it will fine Match Group €11 million ($10 million) as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request. The investigation was launched in January 2020. "The Download My Data tool was presented to Tinder users as a way to request a copy of their personal data," the Data Protection Commission (DPC) said. "It failed to provide users with all of their personal data. Certain categories of information were omitted without notice to the user, or provided in summary form only." In addition to the fine, Match Group has been ordered to bring its processing into compliance within three months. - Rapid-fire domain impersonation Malicious actors registered one-letter lookalikes of new domains for a number of major brands a day after each real domain was registered. "Every lookalike was registered within the next working day of its authentic counterpart, which suggests the actors monitored new registrations made through brand-protection registrars," Broadcom said. history.summary: This week's security highlights include Google's Gemini 4 Neon model improving secure code generation, a $500 million ransomware extortion case leading to the extradition of Roman Khlynovskiy, and the emergence of BubbleLoader malware that hijacks legitimate software via PNGs to deliver payloads. Other notable events are a €11 million Tinder data privacy penalty, EU sanctions against Russian disinformation operations, and a large-scale phishing campaign exploiting the Microsoft 365 outage. Fix: WordPress released version 7.1.5 with security fixes and backported patches to eligible branches.
